newsitem.title: GERMANY: Solana says pact does not prevent NATO action.
newsitem.headline: Solana says pact does not prevent NATO action.

text.p: NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said on Friday that a new security accord with Russia did not formally prevent the alliance acting in new member countries.
The NATO-Russia "Founding Act" is intended to defuse Russian opposition to NATO's planned expansion into states in Eastern Europe that once formed part of the Soviet bloc.
Some western analysts fear the pact, approved on Friday by the 16 NATO members, could tie NATO's hands or create a second-class status for new members.
But Solana told reporters in Bonn after a meeting with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel:
"We will of course be able to utilise the infrastructure of the alliance to carry out NATO missions -- for mutual defence and also for peacekeeping missions."

NATO emphasises in the document that it has no plan, intent or need to station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members. It has also said it foresees no need to station troops from other alliance members there.

Solana said Russia's concerns about NATO military activity so close to its borders had been met by the consultation mechanisms set up under the act. NATO insists this does not give Russia veto rights.
He also emphasised the importance of revisions to be negotiated to the treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe which will aim to allay Russian fears.

Solana said he was confident that a similar accord being negotiated between NATO and Ukraine would be ready in time to be signed at a NATO summit in Madrid in early July, and might even be ready for foreign ministers to initial when they meet in Portugal at the end of this month.

Kinkel insisted that no agreement had been reached with Russia which would prejudice the ability of the three Baltic states -- Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia -- to join NATO at some time in the future.
"We won't accept a closed door or a closed shop after the first wave of new entrants," he said.
The leading candidates for the first wave are widely believed to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
While Russia objects to any eastward enlargement of NATO, it is even more determined to ensure the Baltic states, until recently ruled from Moscow, should not join.
